tagline: A landscaped island approach with protected marsh between mainland and resort
intro: US 278’s Hilton Head Island Scenic Byway is a busy, multilane drive from SC 170 to Sea Pines Circle. The South Carolina Department of Transportation describes a 22-mile route with landscaped medians and broad views, where local limits on signs, setbacks and density have moderated commercial development. Between the mainland and Hilton Head, Pinckney Island National Wildlife Refuge includes salt marsh, tidal creeks, forest and freshwater ponds. The state designated the SC 170–Sea Pines Circle corridor in 2012.

Before 1956, Hilton Head could be reached only by private boat or state ferry. The James F. Byrnes Bridge opened the island to mainland automobile traffic that year. In 1957, Charles E. Fraser and Joseph B. Fraser Jr. formed the Sea Pines Company, initially working from a trailer at Sea Pines Circle. A barge struck the earlier bridge in 1974, stopping vehicle traffic until Army engineers supplied a pontoon crossing during repairs. The original two-lane swing bridge was replaced by a four-lane bridge in 1982.

From SC 170, the approach passes Rose Hill in Bluffton before reaching Pinckney Island between the mainland and Hilton Head. On the island, the scenic corridor continues to Sea Pines Circle, where William Hilton Parkway, Palmetto Bay Road, Pope Avenue and Greenwood Drive meet.

moments.title: Rose Hill Plantation House
moments.text: Rose Hill’s Gothic house was begun before the Civil War and finished after World War II. Work began in 1858, before the Civil War interrupted construction. The Kirk family’s wealth came from enslaved people who grew cotton, rice and indigo on the plantation. In 1946, new owners hired architect Willis Irvin Sr. to renovate the unfinished house. A later fire badly damaged the interior; restoration began again after a 1996 purchase. Its National Register description identifies vertical board-and-batten siding and a steep gabled roof. In 1996, the Middleton White Foundation bought the house and began restoring it as a private home.

moments.title: Pinckney Island National Wildlife Refuge
moments.text: Salt marsh and tidal creeks make up nearly 67 percent of Pinckney Island National Wildlife Refuge. Its ponds and woods also reflect deliberate changes to the land. The Pinckney family cleared maritime forest for a plantation worked by enslaved people. After purchasing the property in 1937, the Bruce family planted trees and built ponds for waterfowl and irrigation. Later owners donated the islands to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service in 1975. The refuge was established on December 4 of that year. The refuge includes ten miles of hiking trails; Pinckney is the only island open to public use.

moments.title: Sea Pines Circle
moments.text: Sea Pines Circle was the starting point for a company as well as the endpoint of today’s scenic byway. The Sea Pines Company’s first offices occupied a trailer here after its formation in 1957. Charles Fraser initially envisioned selling oceanfront and ocean-oriented lots. Architect Stuart O. Dawson’s T-shaped roads arranged rows of seaside houses, while golf courses helped draw residential development into the island’s interior. The circle joins William Hilton Parkway, Palmetto Bay Road, Pope Avenue and Greenwood Drive. By 1967, Fraser had been developing 5,200 acres on Hilton Head for ten years.
